source.title: The Enchiridion
source.attribution: Epictetus, The Enchiridion (trans. George Long), Standard Ebooks, public domain
source.notes: The Enchiridion (Manual) as published in Epictetus, Short Works (trans. George Long), Standard Ebooks. Compiled by Arrian from Epictetus's teaching, c. 135 CE.

cards.title: Sort everything into what is up to you and what is not
cards.body:
Epictetus opens his manual with a split. Your opinions, intentions, desires and choices are yours to direct. Your body, possessions, reputation and job title can be influenced but never fully controlled.

Most stress comes from treating the second group as if it belonged in the first: needing the promotion, the praise, the perfect outcome. Put your effort where your control is real, such as preparation, honesty and how you respond, and hold everything else more loosely.
cards.quote: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
cards.apply_it: Take one worry and split it into two columns: what I control and what I don't. Act on one item from the first column today.

quiz.question: Which of these did Epictetus place among the things in our power?
quiz.explanation: He listed opinion, impulse, desire and aversion as ours; body, property and reputation are not fully in our power.

cards.title: When told someone criticised you, answer with humour, not a defence
cards.body:
Hearing that someone spoke badly of you tempts you to build a case: explain, correct, retaliate. Epictetus suggests a lighter move. Reply that they clearly don't know you well, or they would have mentioned your other faults too.

The joke does real work. It shows you aren't rattled, it quietly admits you are imperfect, and it stops gossip from turning into a feud. Most secondhand criticism loses its power when you refuse to treat it as an emergency.
cards.quote: If a man has reported to you, that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make any defence (answer) to what has been told you: but reply, The man did not know the rest of my faults, for he would not have mentioned these only.
cards.apply_it: Next time you hear secondhand criticism, skip the rebuttal. Try a light, self-aware response, or simply say "Maybe so" and move on.

quiz.question: How did Epictetus suggest responding when told someone spoke ill of you?
options: Say they did not know your other faults
quiz.explanation: His good-humoured reply defuses the remark without a defence.

cards.title: Every situation has two handles: pick it up by the one you can carry
cards.body:
Epictetus says each thing can be grasped by two handles. Seize your brother's unfair behaviour by the handle "he wronged me" and it can't be borne. Seize it by "he is my brother, we grew up together" and suddenly you can carry it.

This isn't excusing bad behaviour. It's choosing which true fact to hold first. With a partner, parent or teammate who lets you down, starting from the relationship rather than the grievance makes a fair, steady response possible.
cards.quote: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who frustrated you recently. Write one true thing about your bond with them, and start your next conversation from there.

quiz.question: In the "two handles" image, what should you grab when your brother acts unjustly?
options: The fact that he is your brother
quiz.explanation: Holding the situation by the bond you share makes it bearable.

cards.title: When a temptation appears, make it wait and picture the after
cards.body:
When a pleasure pulls at you, Epictetus advises a pause. Let it wait. Then imagine two scenes: enjoying it, and the moment afterwards when you might regret it. Set beside those the satisfaction of having said no.

This is a practical brake for late-night snacking, impulse buys or the endless scroll. The delay weakens the urge, and picturing the after-feeling gives your judgement a vote. Sometimes you'll still choose yes, but deliberately rather than by default.
cards.quote: guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part.
cards.apply_it: The next time an impulse hits today, wait ten minutes and picture how you'll feel an hour after giving in. Then decide.

quiz.question: What first step did Epictetus recommend when a pleasure tempts you?
options: Give in quickly to get it over with
Let it wait and allow yourself a delay
quiz.explanation: Delay gives reason time to weigh the pleasure against its aftermath.

cards.title: Describe what people do before you judge whether it is wrong
cards.body:
If someone drinks a lot, Epictetus says, call it drinking a lot, not drinking badly. You don't yet know their reasons, so the label "badly" is a guess wearing the costume of a fact.

Separating observation from evaluation is a small habit with big effects. "She left the meeting early" invites curiosity; "she's so rude" shuts it down. Describing first keeps you accurate, fairer to others and less likely to stir up anger over a story you invented.
cards.quote: Does a man drink much wine? do not say that he does this badly, but say that he drinks much. For before you shall have determined the opinion, how do you know whether he is acting wrong?
cards.apply_it: Catch one judgement you make about someone today and restate it as a plain description of what they did.

quiz.question: Why did Epictetus advise saying a man "drinks much" rather than "drinks badly"?
options: Because you do not yet know whether he is acting wrongly
quiz.explanation: Until you know his reasons, a judgement goes beyond what you have actually observed.

cards.title: Stop scheduling your self-improvement for a future date
cards.body:
Epictetus scolds the student who keeps setting dates for when he'll finally take himself seriously: next week, after this project, once things calm down. You're an adult already, he says. Waiting for the right teacher or moment is just another delay.

The promise to start later feels like progress but changes nothing. Improvement only happens in the present day's choices. Pick one standard you already believe in and begin living by it now, imperfectly.
cards.quote: How long will you then still defer thinking yourself worthy of the best things, and in no matter transgressing the distinctive reason? … You are no longer a youth, but already a full-grown man.
cards.apply_it: Name one change you keep postponing to "someday". Do the smallest version of it before tonight.

quiz.question: What was Epictetus criticising in this passage?
quiz.explanation: He challenges the habit of setting day after day for when you will attend to yourself.

cards.title: It is your opinion about events that upsets you, not the events
cards.body:
Epictetus says people are troubled less by what happens than by the story they tell themselves about it. The same event can crush one person and barely touch another, because their judgements differ.

He also describes three stages of growth. A beginner blames other people for his troubles. Someone learning starts to look at his own reactions. Someone well trained blames nobody at all, and simply works on his judgements. When you feel upset, look first at the opinion underneath the feeling.
cards.quote: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel upset, write the event in one line and your judgement of it in another. Ask whether the judgement is the only possible one.

quiz.question: According to Epictetus, what does a person whose training is complete do when things go wrong?
options: Blames the people who caused it
quiz.explanation: He describes three stages: blaming others, blaming yourself, and finally blaming neither, while you work on your own opinions.

cards.title: Want things to happen as they actually happen
cards.body:
Much of our frustration comes from a gap between what we demanded and what reality delivered. Epictetus offers a short, radical fix: stop insisting that events follow your wishes, and instead align your wishes with events.

This is not laziness or giving up on effort. You still act, plan and try. But once something has already happened, such as the rain, the delay, the rejection, fighting it in your head only adds pain. Accepting it frees your energy for the next useful step.
cards.quote: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing today that has already happened and annoyed you. Say to yourself, "This is how it is," then name one next step.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus suggest instead of wishing events would go your way?
options: Wish for events to be as they are
quiz.explanation: He says to wish things to be as they are; then life flows more calmly. It is about accepting what has already happened, not about giving up effort.

cards.title: Before any activity, picture what it usually involves
cards.body:
Epictetus uses the example of going to the public baths: people splash, push, insult each other and even steal. If you go in expecting all this, you won't be thrown when it happens.

The lesson works for a bus ride, a family visit or a busy market. Before you start, remind yourself what the activity is really like, and add a second aim: to stay calm and decent while doing it. Then if things go wrong, you can still achieve the second aim, even when the first is blocked.
cards.quote: When you are going to take in hand any act, remind yourself what kind of an act it is.
cards.apply_it: Before your next meeting or trip, spend 30 seconds imagining the likely annoyances, and decide now how you want to respond to them.

quiz.question: In Epictetus' bath example, what second aim should you hold besides bathing?
options: Keeping your will in harmony with nature, staying calm
Making sure nobody steals from you
quiz.explanation: He says: I intend to bathe, and also to keep my will in a natural state. If the bath goes badly, the second aim can still be met.

cards.title: For every challenge, ask which strength it is calling on
cards.body:
Epictetus advises that whenever something happens to you, you turn inward and ask what ability you have for dealing with it. Temptation calls on self-control. Hard work or pain calls on endurance. Insults call on patience.

This turns each difficulty into a training exercise rather than a threat. Over time the habit becomes automatic, and passing impressions stop dragging you along. You start to see that you are better equipped than you thought; you just needed to remember which tool to pick up.
cards.quote: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
cards.apply_it: Think of a difficulty you face this week. Name the one strength it asks of you (patience, endurance, courage, self-control) and practise it there.

quiz.question: According to Epictetus, which power do abusive words call on?
quiz.explanation: He pairs temptation with temperance, labour with endurance, and abusive words with patience.

cards.title: Small losses are the price you pay for peace of mind
cards.body:
Epictetus suggests starting your training with little things. Some oil gets spilled, a bit of wine goes missing. Instead of getting worked up, tell yourself: this is what calm costs, and nothing comes for free.

It is a useful way to frame minor annoyances today: the lost pen, the overcharged taxi, the colleague who forgot. Fighting every small loss costs you far more in stress than the loss itself. Choosing to let it go is a fair trade for a settled mind.
cards.quote: Begin then from little things. Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing.
cards.apply_it: When the next small thing goes wrong today, say quietly, "That is the price of my calm," and move on.

quiz.question: Where does Epictetus suggest beginning your practice of calm?
options: With little things, like spilled oil
With the death of a loved one
quiz.explanation: He says to begin from little things. Small losses are cheap practice and teach you that tranquillity has a price.

cards.title: Be willing to look foolish while you are improving
cards.body:
Epictetus warns that you cannot chase inner progress and outside approval with equal energy. If you want to improve, you must accept looking naive or out of step about things other people care about.

He even says that if people start to treat you as important, you should be suspicious of yourself. Growth often looks awkward from the outside: the beginner's questions, the habits others don't understand. Choose the growth, and let the image take care of itself.
cards.quote: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.
cards.apply_it: Ask one "basic" question this week that you have been too proud to ask.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus say you should do if you seem important to others?
options: Use it to gain more influence
quiz.explanation: He says that if you seem to some to be a person of importance, you should distrust yourself, because chasing outside status pulls against inner progress.

cards.title: Treat life like a shared meal: take your portion politely, don't grab
cards.body:
Epictetus compares life to a banquet where dishes are passed around. When a dish reaches you, take a fair portion. If it passes you by, don't hold onto it. If it hasn't come yet, don't reach across the table or let your desire run ahead.

He applies this to family, jobs and wealth. Opportunities arrive in their own time. Grabbing and fretting makes you look greedy and feel anxious, while patience and good manners let you enjoy what does come.
cards.quote: Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it.
cards.apply_it: Name one thing you are impatiently waiting for. What would it look like to wait for it "at the table" rather than reaching for it?

quiz.question: In Epictetus' banquet image, what should you do with a dish that hasn't reached you yet?
options: Ask someone to pass it quickly
Wait until it comes to you
quiz.explanation: He says do not send your desire forward to it; wait until it is in front of you.

cards.title: Show sympathy to people in grief without being swept away yourself
cards.body:
When someone you know is weeping over a loss, Epictetus says you should not refuse them sympathy. Speak kindly, and even share their tears if the moment calls for it.

But inside, keep your footing. Remind yourself that their pain comes from how they see the event, and that you will be more useful to them steady than collapsed. This is a healthy model for supporting others: be warm and present, but don't take on their distress as if it were your own.
cards.quote: So far as words then do not be unwilling to show him sympathy, and even if it happens so, to lament with him. But take care that you do not lament internally also.
cards.apply_it: Next time you comfort someone, focus on listening and kind words, and notice whether you can stay calm inside while you do it.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus advise when someone near you is grieving?
options: Show sympathy, but don't lament inside
Tell them their pain is foolish
Grieve with them as deeply as they do
quiz.explanation: He says you may show sympathy and even lament with them in words, but take care not to lament internally as well.

cards.title: You didn't pick your role, but you can play it well
cards.body:
Epictetus compares life to a play. The writer hands out the parts: some short, some long, a poor man, a ruler, a person with a disability, a private citizen. You did not choose your part.

Your job is to perform it well. This shifts attention away from envying someone else's role and toward excellence in your own. Whatever your situation, whether student, parent, trader or nurse, there is a way to play it with skill and dignity.
cards.quote: For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
cards.apply_it: Write down one role you hold today. What would playing it excellently look like this week?

quiz.question: In Epictetus' play metaphor, what is your duty?
options: To choose the best part available
To act well the part you are given
quiz.explanation: He says your duty is to act well the part given to you; selecting the part belongs to someone else.

cards.title: Only enter contests you control and you can't be beaten
cards.body:
Epictetus says you can be unbeatable if you only compete where winning depends on you. Being honest, patient or hard-working is up to you; being the richest or most famous is not.

He adds that when you see someone honoured or powerful, don't assume they are happy. If you believe the real good lies in your own choices, envy and jealousy lose their grip. You stop measuring yourself against other people's luck and start measuring yourself against your own standards.
cards.quote: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you feel envy. Ask: is the thing I envy really in my power? If not, what contest can I enter instead?

quiz.question: How can you be invincible, according to Epictetus?
options: By entering only contests you have the power to win
quiz.explanation: He says you are invincible if you enter no contest that it is not in your power to win.

cards.title: Expect mockery when you change, and hold steady
cards.body:
Epictetus warns anyone who starts living by new principles to expect ridicule. People will say you've suddenly become superior and question where your new attitude came from.

His advice: don't actually act superior, but don't drop your principles either. If you stay steady, those who mocked you often come to respect you. If you give in, you get laughed at twice: once for changing and again for quitting. This applies to anyone starting a new habit, faith, diet or career path.
cards.quote: And remember that if you abide in the same principles, these men who first ridiculed will afterwards admire you: but if you shall have been overpowered by them, you will bring on yourself double ridicule.
cards.apply_it: Think of a change you are making. Prepare one calm sentence to reply with when someone teases you about it.

quiz.question: What happens, according to Epictetus, if you give in to people who mock your new principles?
options: You bring double ridicule on yourself
quiz.explanation: He says those who ridicule you may later admire you if you hold firm, but if you are overpowered you bring double ridicule on yourself.

cards.title: Don't trade your integrity for money, even to help others
cards.body:
Friends may say: get rich so we can benefit too. Epictetus answers that he will happily earn money if he can do it while staying honest, modest and loyal. But if earning means losing those qualities, the deal is unfair.

He asks which you would rather have: money, or a faithful and modest friend. He also argues you serve your community best by being a trustworthy person, not by sacrificing your character for status. Money is welcome, but never at the price of who you are.
cards.quote: If I can acquire money and also keep myself modest, and faithful and magnanimous, point out the way, and I will acquire it.
cards.apply_it: Is there an opportunity in front of you that would pay but cost you honesty? Write down what you would be giving up.

quiz.question: When friends urge him to get rich, what condition does Epictetus set?
options: Only if it can be done quickly
Only if they share the profits
Only if he can stay modest, faithful and magnanimous
quiz.explanation: He says he will acquire money if someone shows him how to do it while keeping his modesty, faithfulness and magnanimity.

cards.title: Everything has a price; if you didn't pay it, don't resent missing out
cards.body:
Someone else got the invitation, the promotion or the attention. Epictetus asks: what did they pay for it? Perhaps flattery, constant visits, or praise for a powerful person.

His example is lettuce at the market. The person who paid has the lettuce; you kept your coin. Neither of you is worse off. If you refuse to pay the price, whether it is money, flattery or time, you can't fairly complain about not getting the goods. What you have instead is your self-respect and the freedom of not having flattered anyone.
cards.quote: If then a man gives up the obolus, and receives the lettuces, and if you do not give up the obolus and do not obtain the lettuces, do not suppose that you receive less than he who has got the lettuces
cards.apply_it: Think of something someone else got that you didn't. Write down the price they paid. Would you actually pay it?

quiz.question: In Epictetus' lettuce example, what does the person who didn't buy the lettuce still have?
options: The coin they did not spend
quiz.explanation: He says the buyer has the lettuce and you have the obol you didn't give, so you are not worse off. The same applies to status won by flattery.

cards.title: React to your own misfortune as you would to a neighbour's
cards.body:
When a neighbour's cup breaks, we shrug: these things happen. When our own breaks, it feels like a disaster. Epictetus says the calm we show about other people's mishaps is the right standard for our own.

He extends this, gently, to bigger losses too. We easily say that such events are part of human life when they happen to others. Remembering how we view them from the outside can help us keep perspective when they happen to us, and stop us adding self-pity to pain.
cards.quote: You must know then that when your cup also is broken, you ought to think as you did when your neighbour’s cup was broken.
cards.apply_it: Next time something of yours breaks or goes wrong, ask: what would I say if this happened to my neighbour?

quiz.question: What standard does Epictetus suggest for reacting to your own broken cup?
options: Be as upset as the cup was valuable
Find out who is to blame
React as you did when your neighbour's cup broke
quiz.explanation: He says that when your own cup breaks, you should think as you did when your neighbour's cup broke: it is one of the things that happen.

cards.title: Don't hand your peace of mind to any stranger who insults you
cards.body:
Epictetus offers a sharp comparison. You would be furious if someone handed your body over to any passer-by. Yet when you let a stranger's insult disturb and upset you, you have handed over your mind just as easily.

It is a useful question for modern life, from road rage to online comments. Who are you allowing to control your mood today? You can hear rude words without giving the speaker the keys to your inner state.
cards.quote: but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?
cards.apply_it: Count how many times today a stranger, driver or online comment changed your mood. Choose one you will not give that power to tomorrow.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus compare letting a stranger's insult disturb you to?
options: Putting your body in the power of anyone you meet
Breaking a promise to a friend
quiz.explanation: He says we'd be vexed if our body were put in the power of anyone we met, so we should be ashamed to put our understanding in their power.

cards.title: Count the full cost before you commit to a goal
cards.body:
Epictetus describes someone who wants to win at the Olympic games. Fine, he says, but look at what comes first and what follows: strict diet, training in heat and cold, injuries, and after all that, perhaps defeat.

If you still want it after considering this, go ahead. If not, you'll be like children who play athlete one day and musician the next, never committing to anything. Before starting a degree, a business or a training plan, look honestly at the price. Then choose with your whole self.
cards.quote: In every act observe the things which come first, and those which follow it; and so proceed to the act.
cards.apply_it: Write down a goal you're considering, then list the three hardest things it will demand. Decide if you will truly accept them.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus say happens to people who start things without considering the costs?
options: They jump from one thing to another and become nothing
quiz.explanation: He compares them to children who play at one role after another: undertaking things carelessly, they end up being nothing at all with their whole soul.

cards.title: Let your relationships, not others' behaviour, guide your conduct
cards.body:
Epictetus says our duties come from our relationships: as a child, sibling, neighbour or citizen. If your brother treats you unfairly, the question isn't what he is doing, but what you should do to act well.

This doesn't mean accepting harm or abuse; it means not letting someone else's poor behaviour lower your own standards. Your conduct stays your own. As he puts it, another person cannot really damage you unless you decide you've been damaged.
cards.quote: Does a brother wrong you? Maintain then your own position towards him, and do not examine what he is doing, but what you must do
cards.apply_it: Think of a relative who has disappointed you. Ask: given our relationship, what is the decent thing for me to do next?

quiz.question: When a brother wrongs you, what does Epictetus say to focus on?
options: What you must do to act well
How to get even with him
Whether others agree he was wrong
quiz.explanation: He says not to examine what the brother is doing, but what you must do so that your own will stays in line with nature.

cards.title: Speak less, and avoid talking about people behind their backs
cards.body:
Epictetus advises a habit of quiet: say what is needed, in few words. He especially warns against chatter about other people, blaming them, praising them or comparing them.

Gossip and constant commentary drain attention and damage trust. If you can, steer conversations toward something worthwhile; if you're among people where that isn't possible, silence is fine. Fewer words often carry more weight, and people learn that what you say is worth hearing.
cards.quote: and especially not about men, as blaming them or praising them, or comparing them.
cards.apply_it: In your next group conversation, notice when talk turns to judging someone absent. Try changing the subject, or simply stay quiet.

quiz.question: Which kind of talk does Epictetus especially warn against?
quiz.explanation: He says to speak little, and especially not about people: blaming them, praising them or comparing them.

cards.title: Before approaching powerful people, expect the door to stay shut
cards.body:
When you go to see someone important, Epictetus says to prepare for the worst: they won't be in, you'll be turned away, they won't care about you. If it is still your duty to go, go anyway and accept what happens.

And never tell yourself afterwards that it wasn't worth the effort. That complaint shows you were really there for the outcome, not for doing your part. For job seekers, salespeople and anyone asking for help, this mindset makes rejection much easier to carry.
cards.quote: And if with all this it is your duty to visit him, bear what happens, and never say to yourself that it was not worth the trouble.
cards.apply_it: Before your next pitch or request, write: "They may say no or ignore me. I'll do my part well anyway."

quiz.question: After a visit to a powerful person goes badly, what does Epictetus say you should never tell yourself?
options: That it was not worth the trouble
quiz.explanation: He says it is silly to tell yourself it wasn't worth the trouble; that marks someone who is upset by externals.

cards.title: If something is right to do, do it openly, whatever people think
cards.body:
Epictetus gives a simple test. If an action is wrong, don't do it. If it is right, why fear people who will criticise you wrongly?

Many of us do good things secretly or not at all because we fear looking odd: leaving a party early, refusing a bribe, studying while friends go out. Once you've thought it through and decided it's right, hiding it only gives power to opinions that are mistaken.
cards.quote: For if it is not right to do it, avoid doing the thing; but if it is right, why are you afraid of those who shall find fault wrongly?
cards.apply_it: Is there a good habit you hide from others out of embarrassment? Do it openly once this week.

quiz.question: What is Epictetus' test for whether to fear being seen doing something?
options: If it's right, don't fear those who criticise wrongly
Do it only when nobody is watching
quiz.explanation: He says if it's not right, don't do it; if it is right, there is no reason to fear those who wrongly find fault.

cards.title: Let real needs set the limit on what you own
cards.body:
Epictetus says the body is the measure of what you need, just as the foot is the measure of the shoe. Stay with that measure and you stay balanced.

Go past it and there's no natural stopping point: first a gilded shoe, then a purple one, then an embroidered one. This is an early description of lifestyle creep. Once spending is driven by show rather than need, every upgrade makes the next one feel necessary. Anchoring purchases to real needs protects both your wallet and your peace.
cards.quote: The measure of possession (property) is to every man the body, as the foot is of the shoe.
cards.apply_it: Before your next non-essential purchase, ask: which real need does this meet? If none, wait a week.

quiz.question: In Epictetus' shoe example, what happens once you go past the foot's needs?
options: There is no limit: gilded, purple, then embroidered
quiz.explanation: He says once you pass the true measure, the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then embroidered, because there is no limit beyond it.

cards.title: When someone wrongs you, remember it seemed right to them
cards.body:
Epictetus notes that people who treat you badly usually act on what they think is right. They can only follow their own view, not yours. If their view is mistaken, they are the ones harmed, because they've been deceived.

Seeing it this way makes you gentler with people who insult or cross you. Instead of building a case against them, you can say simply: it seemed so to him. That doesn't mean agreeing; it means not adding your anger to their mistake.
cards.quote: If you proceed then from these opinions, you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you: for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who annoyed you recently. Try to state their reasoning in a way they would agree with.

quiz.question: What phrase does Epictetus suggest saying when someone reviles you?
quiz.explanation: He suggests saying "It seemed so to him": people act on what seems right to them, and recognising this makes you milder.

cards.title: Being richer or smarter doesn't make you a better person
cards.body:
Epictetus points out a faulty line of reasoning: "I'm richer than you, so I'm better than you." The correct conclusion is only that your possessions are greater. Being more eloquent means your speech is better, not you.

You are not your bank balance or your talents. Remembering this works in both directions: it keeps you humble when you're ahead, and stops you feeling small when someone else has more money, skill or status than you.
cards.quote: I am richer than you, therefore my possessions are greater than yours: I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is superior to yours. But you are neither possession nor speech.
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you feel superior or inferior to someone. Rephrase it the way Epictetus would: "My X is greater than theirs," not "I am."

quiz.question: What does "I am richer than you" correctly lead to, according to Epictetus?
options: My possessions are greater than yours
quiz.explanation: He says the reasoning that coheres is only that your possessions are greater; you are neither your possessions nor your speech.

cards.title: Show what you've learned through your actions, not lectures
cards.body:
Epictetus tells us not to call ourselves philosophers or lecture people on how they should live. At a dinner, don't explain how to eat properly; just eat properly.

He uses a vivid image: sheep don't bring up their grass to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest it and produce wool and milk. In the same way, the proof of what you've read is how you behave. Lecturing too early often means you haven't absorbed the lesson yet.
cards.quote: Do you also show not your theorems to the uninstructed, but show the acts which come from their digestion.
cards.apply_it: Pick one idea from a book you liked. Instead of telling someone about it this week, quietly put it into practice.

quiz.question: What does Epictetus say sheep do instead of showing how much grass they've eaten?
options: They eat more in front of the shepherd
They digest it and produce wool and milk
